rules.message: 'Information' is uncountable: it has no plural form.
rules.bad: I need some informations about the trip.
rules.good: I need some information about the trip.
rules.fixed: I need some information about the trip.

rules.message: 'Advice' is uncountable: it has no plural form. You can say 'some advice' or 'a piece of advice'.
rules.bad: Can you give me some advices?
rules.good: Can you give me some advice?
rules.fixed: Can you give me some advice?

rules.message: 'Furniture' is uncountable: it has no plural form.
rules.bad: We bought new furnitures for the flat.
rules.good: We bought new furniture for the flat.
rules.fixed: We bought new furniture for the flat.

rules.message: 'Homework' is uncountable: it has no plural form.
rules.bad: I have a lot of homeworks today.
rules.good: I have a lot of homework today.
rules.fixed: I have a lot of homework today.

rules.message: 'Knowledge' is uncountable: it has no plural form.
rules.bad: She has great knowledges of history.
rules.good: She has great knowledge of history.
rules.fixed: She has great knowledge of history.

rules.message: This noun is uncountable: it has no plural form.
rules.bad: Please carry your luggages to the car.
rules.good: Please carry your luggage to the car.
rules.fixed: Please carry your luggage to the car.

rules.message: You cannot use 'a' or 'an' with an uncountable noun. Use 'some' or 'a piece of'.
rules.bad: He gave me an advice about the exam.
rules.good: He gave me a piece of advice about the exam.
rules.fixed: He gave me some advice about the exam.

rules.message: Use 'much' or 'a lot of' with uncountable nouns, not 'many'.
rules.bad: I do not have many time today.
rules.good: I do not have much time today.
rules.fixed: I do not have a lot of time today.

rules.message: Use 'many' with plural countable nouns, not 'much'.
rules.bad: There were much people at the party.
rules.good: There were many people at the party.
rules.fixed: There were many people at the party.

rules.message: After 'a lot' and 'lots' you need 'of'.
rules.bad: I met a lot people at the festival.
rules.good: I met a lot of people at the festival.
rules.fixed: I met a lot of people at the festival.

rules.message: 'People' is plural, so you cannot use 'a' before it. Use 'a person' or 'people'.
rules.bad: A people told me the way.
rules.good: A person told me the way.
rules.fixed: A person told me the way.

rules.message: 'People' and 'police' are plural, so use 'are' or 'were'.
rules.bad: The people is very friendly here.
rules.good: One of the people is very friendly here.
rules.fixed: The people are very friendly here.

rules.message: 'News' is uncountable, so use 'is' or 'was'.
rules.bad: The news are good today.
rules.good: The news is good today.
rules.fixed: The news is good today.

rules.message: The plural of 'child' is 'children'.
rules.bad: The childs are playing outside.
rules.good: The children are playing outside.
rules.fixed: The children are playing outside.

rules.message: 'Children' is already plural, so it does not take an -s.
rules.bad: My childrens like football.
rules.good: My children like football.
rules.fixed: My children like football.

rules.message: Adjectives do not take a plural -s in English.
rules.bad: We visited many differents places.
rules.good: We visited many different places.
rules.fixed: We visited many different places.

rules.message: 'Agree' is a verb, so you do not need 'am'. Say 'I agree'.
rules.bad: I am agree with you.
rules.good: I agree with you.
rules.fixed: I agree with you.

rules.message: Say 'I do not agree' or 'I disagree'.
rules.bad: I am not agree with this idea.
rules.good: I do not agree with this idea.
rules.fixed: I don't agree with this idea.

rules.message: We say 'depend on', not 'depend of'.
rules.bad: It depends of the weather.
rules.good: It depends on the weather.
rules.fixed: It depends on the weather.

rules.message: After 'explain' you need 'to' before the person: 'explain to me'.
rules.bad: Can you explain me the rules?
rules.good: Can you explain to me the rules?
rules.fixed: Can you explain to me the rules?

rules.message: We say 'married to' someone.
rules.bad: She is married with a doctor.
rules.good: She is married to a doctor.
rules.fixed: She is married to a doctor.

rules.message: 'Marry' does not need 'with'. We marry someone.
rules.bad: He wants to marry with her.
rules.good: He wants to marry her.
rules.fixed: He wants to marry her.

rules.message: 'Discuss' does not need 'about'.
rules.bad: We discussed about the plan.
rules.good: We discussed the plan.
rules.fixed: We discussed the plan.

rules.message: We say 'arrive at' a place or 'arrive in' a city or country.
rules.bad: We arrived to the station at six.
rules.good: We arrived at the station at six.
rules.fixed: We arrived at the station at six.

rules.message: 'Enter' does not need 'in'. We enter a place.
rules.bad: She entered in the room.
rules.good: She entered the room.
rules.fixed: She entered the room.

rules.message: We 'take' photos. We do not 'make' or 'do' them.
rules.bad: We made a lot of photos on the beach.
rules.good: We took a lot of photos on the beach.
rules.fixed: We took a lot of photos on the beach.

rules.message: We 'have' or 'throw' a party. We do not 'make' it.
rules.bad: I will make a party on Saturday.
rules.good: I will have a party on Saturday.
rules.fixed: I will have a party on Saturday.

rules.message: We 'do' homework, housework, sport and exercise. We do not 'make' them.
rules.bad: I make my homework after dinner.
rules.good: I do my homework after dinner.
rules.fixed: I do my homework after dinner.

rules.message: We 'take' or 'do' an exam. We do not 'make' one.
rules.bad: I made the exam last week.
rules.good: I took the exam last week.
rules.fixed: I took the exam last week.

rules.message: We 'ask' a question. We do not 'make' one.
rules.bad: Can I make a question?
rules.good: Can I ask a question?
rules.fixed: Can I ask a question?

rules.message: We 'make' mistakes. We do not 'do' them.
rules.bad: I did many mistakes in the test.
rules.good: I made many mistakes in the test.
rules.fixed: I made many mistakes in the test.

rules.message: Most learners say 'make a decision'. 'Take a decision' is used mainly in British English.
rules.bad: We took a decision yesterday.
rules.good: We made a decision yesterday.
rules.fixed: We made a decision yesterday.

rules.message: Use 'tell' when you say who hears it: 'tell me'. 'Say' needs the words that were said.
rules.bad: He said me the news.
rules.good: He told me the news.
rules.fixed: He told me the news.

rules.message: After 'tell' you do not need 'to' before the person.
rules.bad: She told to me a secret.
rules.good: She told me a secret.
rules.fixed: She told me a secret.

rules.message: Use 'for' with a length of time and 'since' with a starting point.
rules.bad: I have lived here since three years.
rules.good: I have lived here for three years.
rules.fixed: I have lived here for three years.

rules.message: To talk about the period just before now, we say 'last week', not 'the last week'.
rules.bad: I went to London the last week.
rules.good: I went to London last week.
rules.fixed: I went to London last week.

rules.message: In English we say age with 'be': 'I am 20 years old', not 'I have 20 years'.
rules.bad: He has 15 years.
rules.good: He is 15 years old.
rules.fixed: He is 15 years old.

rules.message: In English we say age with 'be': 'my brother is 15 years old', not 'my brother has 15 years'.
rules.bad: My brother has 15 years.
rules.good: My brother is 15 years old.
rules.fixed: My brother is 15 years old.

rules.message: With he, she and it, use 'doesn't'.
rules.bad: She don't like coffee.
rules.good: She doesn't like coffee.
rules.fixed: She doesn't like coffee.

rules.message: With he, she and it, use 'does not'.
rules.bad: He do not know the answer.
rules.good: He does not know the answer.
rules.fixed: He does not know the answer.

rules.message: With he, she and it, use 'has'.
rules.bad: She have a new bike.
rules.good: Does she have a new bike?
rules.fixed: She has a new bike.

rules.message: With he and she in the present simple, the verb needs -s: 'he works', 'she likes'.
rules.bad: She like music.
rules.good: Does she like music?
rules.fixed: She likes music.

rules.message: After a modal verb (can, must, should...) we use the base verb without 'to'.
rules.bad: I can to help you tomorrow.
rules.good: I can help you tomorrow.
rules.fixed: I can help you tomorrow.

rules.message: Use 'to' before the verb: 'want to go', 'would like to visit'.
rules.bad: I want go to the cinema.
rules.good: I want to go to the cinema.
rules.fixed: I want to go to the cinema.

rules.message: We say 'I want you to do something', not 'I want that you do'.
rules.bad: I want that you come to my party.
rules.good: I want you to come to my party.
rules.fixed: I want you to come to my party.

rules.message: After like, love, enjoy and hate, use the -ing form (or 'to' + verb for like, love, hate).
rules.bad: I enjoy swim in the sea.
rules.good: I enjoy swimming in the sea.
rules.fixed: I enjoy swimming in the sea.

rules.message: After this verb use the -ing form, not 'to' + verb.
rules.bad: I enjoy to travel with my family.
rules.good: I enjoy travelling with my family.

rules.pattern: \b(I am|I'm|he is|she is|we are|they are|you are|it is) (study|work|live|play|go|do|watch|read|eat|learn|cook|write|run|sleep|talk|speak|travel|walk|wait|stay|come)\b
rules.message: After 'am', 'is' or 'are' you need the -ing form (or a different structure).
rules.bad: I am study English this year.
rules.good: I am studying English this year.
rules.fixed: I am studying English this year.

rules.message: After 'have' or 'has' use the past participle, for example 'seen', 'gone', 'done'.
rules.bad: I have see that film twice.
rules.good: I have seen that film twice.
rules.fixed: I have seen that film twice.

rules.message: After 'did', 'do' and 'does' the main verb stays in the base form.
rules.bad: I didn't went to school yesterday.
rules.good: I didn't go to school yesterday.
rules.fixed: I didn't go to school yesterday.

rules.message: This is an irregular verb. Its past form is different.
rules.bad: Yesterday we goed to the beach.
rules.good: Yesterday we went to the beach.
rules.fixed: Yesterday we went to the beach.

rules.message: We say 'was born' or 'were born'.
rules.bad: I born in 2008.
rules.good: I was born in 2008.
rules.fixed: I was born in 2008.

rules.message: With 'I' use 'have' and 'am'.
rules.bad: I has a new phone.
rules.good: I have a new phone.
rules.fixed: I have a new phone.

rules.message: With 'they', 'we' and 'you' use 'were'.
rules.bad: They was very tired.
rules.good: They were very tired.
rules.fixed: They were very tired.

rules.pattern: \bthere(?: is|'s) (?=(?:many|several|two|three|four|five|six|seven|eight|nine|ten|a few|a couple of|lots of \w+s|a lot of \w+s)\b)
rules.message: Use 'there are' before a plural.
rules.bad: There is many people in the park.
rules.good: There are many people in the park.
rules.fixed: There are many people in the park.

rules.message: Use 'there is' before a singular noun.
rules.bad: There are a big park near my house.
rules.good: There are a lot of parks near my house.
rules.fixed: There is a big park near my house.

rules.message: To say what exists in a place, use 'there is' or 'there are', not 'have'.
rules.bad: In my city have a lot of parks.
rules.good: In my city there are a lot of parks.

rules.message: After 'look forward to' use the -ing form.
rules.bad: I look forward to see you.
rules.good: I look forward to seeing you.
rules.fixed: I look forward to seeing you.

rules.message: After 'thanks for' use the -ing form or a noun ('thanks for inviting me', 'thanks for the invitation').
rules.bad: Thank you for invite me to your party.
rules.good: Thank you for inviting me to your party.
rules.fixed: Thank you for inviting me to your party.

rules.message: To say why you do something, use 'to' + verb. Do not use 'for to'.
rules.bad: I use this app for to learn English.
rules.good: I use this app to learn English.
rules.fixed: I use this app to learn English.

rules.message: To say why you do something, use 'to' + verb, not 'for' + verb.
rules.bad: I am writing for ask you a question.
rules.good: I am writing to ask you a question.
rules.fixed: I am writing to ask you a question.

rules.message: After 'suggest' we do not use 'someone to do'. Say 'I suggest that you go' or 'I suggest going'.
rules.bad: I suggest you to visit the museum.
rules.good: I suggest that you visit the museum.

rules.message: Put 'very much' after the thing you like: 'I like the film very much'.
rules.bad: I like very much the film.
rules.good: I like the film very much.

rules.pattern: \b(I am|I'm|we are|he is|she is|they are|I was) (living|working|studying|waiting|learning)\b(?=[^.!?]{0,40}\b(?:since|for (?:\d+|two|three|four|five|six|several|a few) (?:years|months|weeks)))
rules.message: With 'since' or 'for' and a time up to now, use the present perfect continuous: 'I have been living'.
rules.bad: I am living here since 2019.
rules.good: I am living here now.

rules.message: Do not use the present perfect with a finished time such as 'yesterday' or 'last week'. Use the past simple.
rules.bad: I have visited my aunt last week.
rules.good: I have visited my aunt many times.

rules.message: With countable nouns we usually say 'fewer'.
rules.bad: There are less people here now.
rules.good: There are fewer people here now.
rules.fixed: There are fewer people here now.

rules.message: This comparative is already complete. Do not add 'more'.
rules.bad: This phone is more better than mine.
rules.good: This phone is better than mine.
rules.fixed: This phone is better than mine.

rules.message: Short adjectives make the comparative with -er: 'taller than', not 'more tall than'.
rules.bad: My brother is more tall than me.
rules.good: My brother is taller than me.
rules.fixed: My brother is taller than me.

rules.message: The comparative of 'good' is 'better' and of 'bad' is 'worse'. The superlatives are 'best' and 'worst'.
rules.bad: This film is more good than the book.
rules.good: This film is better than the book.
rules.fixed: This film is better than the book.

rules.message: Say 'most of the' or 'most of them'. ('Make the most of' is correct.)
rules.bad: The most of my friends live nearby.
rules.good: Most of my friends live nearby.
rules.fixed: Most of my friends live nearby.

rules.message: Say 'most people', without 'the', when you mean 'the majority of people'.
rules.bad: The most people like pizza.
rules.good: Most people like pizza.
rules.fixed: Most people like pizza.

rules.message: Do not use 'the' when you talk about something in general.
rules.bad: The life is short.
rules.good: Life is short.
rules.fixed: Life is short.

rules.message: Do not use 'the' with sports and activities in general.
rules.bad: I love the football.
rules.good: I love football.
rules.fixed: I love football.

rules.message: Do not use 'the' before the name of most countries.
rules.bad: I live in the Spain.
rules.good: I live in Spain.
rules.fixed: I live in Spain.

rules.message: Use 'an' before a vowel sound.
rules.bad: She is a engineer.
rules.good: She is an engineer.
rules.fixed: She is an engineer.

rules.message: Use 'a' before a consonant sound.
rules.bad: He is an teacher.
rules.good: He is an honest teacher.
rules.fixed: He is a teacher.

rules.message: In English the adjective comes before the noun: 'a big house', not 'a house big'.
rules.bad: We have a house big.
rules.good: We have a big house.
rules.fixed: We have a big house.

rules.message: English sentences need a subject. Start with 'It is'.
rules.bad: Is important to sleep well.
rules.good: It is important to sleep well.
rules.fixed: It is important to sleep well.

rules.message: English sentences need a subject. Say 'it is'.
rules.bad: I stayed home because is raining.
rules.good: I stayed home because it is raining.
rules.fixed: I stayed home because it is raining.

rules.message: English sentences need a subject. Start with 'It is'.
rules.bad: Is raining today.
rules.good: It is raining today.
rules.fixed: It is raining today.

rules.message: Use 'what' and give a subject: 'what it is called'.
rules.bad: I do not know how is called.
rules.good: I do not know what it is called.
rules.fixed: I do not know what it is called.

rules.message: Use 'what' to ask for a name: 'What do you call...?'.
rules.bad: How do you call this in English?
rules.good: What do you call this in English?
rules.fixed: What do you call this in English?

rules.message: We say 'interested in'.
rules.bad: I am interested on art.
rules.good: I am interested in art.
rules.fixed: I am interested in art.

rules.message: We say 'good at' a skill or subject.
rules.bad: I am good in maths.
rules.good: I am good at maths.
rules.fixed: I am good at maths.

rules.message: We say 'listen to' something.
rules.bad: I listen music every day.
rules.good: I listen to music every day.
rules.fixed: I listen to music every day.

rules.message: We say 'wait for' someone or something.
rules.bad: I waited the bus for an hour.
rules.good: I waited for the bus for an hour.
rules.fixed: I waited for the bus for an hour.

rules.message: The verb 'visit' does not need 'to'.
rules.bad: We visited to the museum.
rules.good: We visited the museum.
rules.fixed: We visited the museum.

rules.message: We say 'go home', without 'to'.
rules.bad: I went to home after class.
rules.good: I went home after class.
rules.fixed: I went home after class.

rules.message: We say 'at the weekend' (British English) or 'on the weekend' (American English).
rules.bad: We play football in the weekend.
rules.good: We play football at the weekend.
rules.fixed: We play football at the weekend.

rules.message: We say 'in the morning', 'in the afternoon' and 'in the evening'.
rules.bad: I study at the morning.
rules.good: I study in the morning.
rules.fixed: I study in the morning.

rules.message: Use 'on' with days of the week.
rules.bad: The match is in Saturday.
rules.good: The match is on Saturday.
rules.fixed: The match is on Saturday.

rules.message: Use 'in' with months.
rules.bad: My birthday is on June.
rules.good: My birthday is in June.
rules.fixed: My birthday is in June.

rules.message: Use 'for' to say how long something lasts.
rules.bad: I studied English during three years.
rules.good: I studied English for three years.
rules.fixed: I studied English for three years.

rules.message: We say 'think about' or 'think of' someone.
rules.bad: I think in you every day.
rules.good: I think about you every day.
rules.fixed: I think about you every day.

rules.message: We say 'dream about' or 'dream of'.
rules.bad: I dream with a big house.
rules.good: I dream about a big house.
rules.fixed: I dream about a big house.

rules.message: We say 'insist on'.
rules.bad: She insisted in paying.
rules.good: She insisted on paying.
rules.fixed: She insisted on paying.

rules.message: We say 'look at' something.
rules.bad: Look the map, please.
rules.good: Look at the map, please.
rules.fixed: Look at the map, please.

rules.message: We say 'search for' or 'look for' something.
rules.bad: I am searching a job.
rules.good: I am searching for a job.
rules.fixed: I am searching for a job.

rules.message: We say 'different from' (or 'different to' in British English).
rules.bad: My town is different of yours.
rules.good: My town is different from yours.
rules.fixed: My town is different from yours.

rules.message: We say 'similar to'.
rules.bad: Your bag is similar with mine.
rules.good: Your bag is similar to mine.
rules.fixed: Your bag is similar to mine.

rules.message: We say 'the same as'.
rules.bad: She has the same phone than me.
rules.good: She has the same phone as me.
rules.fixed: She has the same phone as me.

rules.message: Say 'despite' (no 'of') or 'in spite of'.
rules.bad: Despite of the rain, we went out.
rules.good: Despite the rain, we went out.
rules.fixed: Despite the rain, we went out.

rules.message: The fixed phrase is 'on the other hand'.
rules.bad: In the other hand, it is expensive.
rules.good: On the other hand, it is expensive.
rules.fixed: On the other hand, it is expensive.

rules.message: We say 'in my opinion'.
rules.bad: On my opinion, it is a good idea.
rules.good: In my opinion, it is a good idea.
rules.fixed: In my opinion, it is a good idea.

rules.message: Use 'in my opinion' or 'I think'. 'According to' is for other people's ideas.
rules.bad: According to me, the film is great.
rules.good: In my opinion, the film is great.
rules.fixed: In my opinion, the film is great.

rules.message: 'It's' (with an apostrophe) means 'it is' or 'it has'.
rules.bad: Its a nice city.
rules.good: It's a nice city.
rules.fixed: It's a nice city.

rules.message: 'Its' (without an apostrophe) shows possession.
rules.bad: The city has it's own style.
rules.good: The city has its own style.
rules.fixed: The city has its own style.

rules.message: 'You're' (with an apostrophe) means 'you are'.
rules.bad: Your very kind.
rules.good: You're very kind.
rules.fixed: You're very kind.

rules.message: 'Their' shows that something belongs to them. 'There' is for places.
rules.bad: They love there house.
rules.good: They love their house.
rules.fixed: They love their house.

rules.message: Use 'there' with 'is' and 'are'.
rules.bad: Their is a park near here.
rules.good: There is a park near here.
rules.fixed: There is a park near here.

rules.message: After a comparative we use 'than'.
rules.bad: He is taller then me.
rules.good: He is taller than me.
rules.fixed: He is taller than me.

rules.message: 'Too' means 'more than you want'. 'To' is a preposition.
rules.bad: The soup is to hot.
rules.good: The soup is too hot.
rules.fixed: The soup is too hot.

rules.message: 'Lose' is the verb. 'Loose' means not tight.
rules.bad: I do not want to loose my keys.
rules.good: I do not want to lose my keys.
rules.fixed: I do not want to lose my keys.

rules.message: This contraction needs an apostrophe.
rules.bad: I dont know the answer.
rules.good: I don't know the answer.
rules.fixed: I don't know the answer.

rules.message: 'A lot' is two words.
rules.bad: I like it alot.
rules.good: I like it a lot.
rules.fixed: I like it a lot.

rules.message: 'Actually' means 'in fact' or 'really'. It does not mean 'at the moment'. For that, use 'currently' or 'at the moment'.
rules.bad: Actually I live in Madrid.
rules.good: Currently I live in Madrid.

rules.message: 'Sensible' means 'reasonable'. If you mean 'easily hurt' or 'feeling things strongly', use 'sensitive'.
rules.bad: She is very sensible and cries easily.
rules.good: She is very sensitive and cries easily.

rules.message: 'Carpet' is a floor covering. For a folder on a computer or at school, use 'folder'.
rules.bad: I put the photos in a carpet.
rules.good: I put the photos in a folder.

rules.message: 'Constipated' is a stomach problem. For a cold, say 'I have a cold'.
rules.bad: I am constipated and I cannot talk.
rules.good: I have a cold and I cannot talk.

rules.message: 'Assist' means 'help'. To go to a class or event, use 'attend'.
rules.bad: I assist to the English class on Monday.
rules.good: I attend the English class on Monday.
rules.fixed: I attend the English class on Monday.

rules.message: 'Pretend' means to act as if something is true. If you plan to do something, say 'I intend to' or 'I want to'.
rules.bad: I pretend to study medicine.
rules.good: I intend to study medicine.
rules.fixed: I intend to study medicine.

rules.message: 'Large' means 'big'. For distance or time, use 'long'.
rules.bad: It was a large trip.
rules.good: It was a long trip.
rules.fixed: It was a long trip.

rules.message: 'Argument' means a disagreement. The story of a film or book is the 'plot'.
rules.bad: The argument of the film is simple.
rules.good: The plot of the film is simple.
rules.fixed: The plot of the film is simple.

rules.message: A 'career' is a job path. At university you study a 'degree' or a 'course'.
rules.bad: I want to study a career in law.
rules.good: I want to study law at university.
rules.fixed: I want to study a degree in law.

rules.message: 'Exit' is a way out. For 'success', use 'success'.
rules.bad: The concert had a great exit.
rules.good: The concert was a great success.
rules.fixed: The concert had a great success.

rules.message: 'Actual' means 'real'. For 'now', use 'current'.
rules.bad: The actual government is new.
rules.good: The current government is new.
rules.fixed: The current government is new.

rules.message: 'Eventually' means 'in the end'. It does not mean 'possibly'. For that, use 'maybe' or 'possibly'.
rules.bad: Eventually I will go.
rules.good: Finally, we arrived at the hotel.

rules.message: 'Sympathetic' means 'understanding when someone is sad'. A friendly person is 'nice' or 'friendly'.
rules.bad: My neighbour is very sympathetic.
rules.good: My neighbour is very friendly.

rules.message: A 'lecture' is a talk given at a university. For 'reading' a book, use 'reading'.
rules.bad: Lecture is my hobby.
rules.good: Reading is my hobby.

rules.message: 'Familiar' means 'well known'. A person in your family is a 'relative'.
rules.bad: I visited my familiar in Paris.
rules.good: I visited my relative in Paris.
rules.fixed: I visited my relative in Paris.

rules.message: 'Fabric' is cloth. A place where things are made is a 'factory'.
rules.bad: My father works in a fabric where they make cars.
rules.good: My father works in a factory where they make cars.
rules.fixed: My father works in a factory where they make cars.

rules.message: 'Contest' means to compete or to disagree. To reply, use 'answer'.
rules.bad: Please contest my email soon.
rules.good: Please answer my email soon.
rules.fixed: Please answer my email soon.

rules.message: To 'support' is to help or hold up. If you do not like something at all, say 'I can't stand it'.
rules.bad: I can't support the noise.
rules.good: I can't stand the noise.
rules.fixed: I can't stand the noise.

rules.message: 'Molest' means to attack someone. If something is annoying you, use 'bother' or 'disturb'.
rules.bad: The noise molested me.
rules.good: The noise bothered me.

rules.pattern: \b(I am|I'm|I was|we were|we are|I feel|I felt) (very |so |really |quite |not )?(boring|interesting|exciting|annoying|tiring|confusing|surprising|worrying|embarrassing)\b
rules.message: Use -ed for how you feel ('I am bored') and -ing for the thing that causes it ('the film is boring').
rules.bad: I was very boring in the lesson.
rules.good: I was very bored in the lesson.
rules.fixed: I was very bored in the lesson.

rules.message: To ask about something you do not understand, say 'I have a question about...'.
rules.bad: I have a doubt about the homework.
rules.good: I have a question about the homework.
rules.fixed: I have a question about the homework.

rules.message: Do not leave a space before a comma, full stop or question mark.
rules.bad: Hello , how are you.
rules.good: Hello, how are you.
rules.fixed: Hello, how are you.

rules.message: Leave a space after a comma.
rules.bad: I like tea,coffee and milk.
rules.good: I like tea, coffee and milk.
rules.fixed: I like tea, coffee and milk.

rules.message: Leave a space after a full stop.
rules.bad: It was great.We had fun.
rules.good: It was great. We had fun.
rules.fixed: It was great. We had fun.

rules.message: The word 'I' is always a capital letter.
rules.bad: Yesterday i went home.
rules.good: Yesterday I went home.
rules.fixed: Yesterday I went home.

rules.message: Use only one space between words.
rules.bad: We  went home.
rules.good: We went home.
rules.fixed: We went home.

rules.message: This word is repeated.
rules.bad: I went to the the park.
rules.good: I went to the park.
rules.fixed: I went to the park.

rules.message: Put a comma after the name in a greeting.
rules.bad:
Dear Alex
Thanks for your email.
rules.good:
Dear Alex,
Thanks for your email.
rules.fixed:
Dear Alex,
Thanks for your email.

rules.message: Put a comma after the name in a greeting.
rules.bad: Hi Alex thanks for your email.
rules.good: Hi Alex, thanks for your email.
rules.fixed: Hi Alex, thanks for your email.

rules.pattern: ^((?:Best wishes|Kind regards|Best regards|Regards|Love|Yours|Cheers|Take care|All the best|Many thanks))[ \t]*$(?=\n\s*\S)
rules.message: Put a comma after the closing phrase.
rules.bad:
Best wishes
Maria
rules.good:
Best wishes,
Maria
rules.fixed:
Best wishes,
Maria
